# Worked example — the counter that killed a deal in four minutes

A real thread, anonymised. Read it as the pattern to recognise, not as a script.

## What happened

A creator with a large audience. A software brand approached them for a sponsored video.

| Stage | Move |
|---|---|
| 1 | Brand emails inbound. Names the deliverables — one dedicated video cross-posted, link in bio for 7 days. Asks for demographics. **States no budget.** |
| 2 | Brand chases. Still no budget stated, and none asked for. |
| 3 | Creator replies with a media kit and nothing else. Correct — the price sits in the PDF, so it is never a number to defend in a sentence. |
| 4 | Brand comes back: **$1,000 flat**, and quietly adds "30 days of ads rights" to the deliverables. |
| 5 | Creator counters **$3,375**. One number. No alternative beside it. |
| 6 | Brand passes. **Four minutes later.** |

Outcome: nothing. And a four-minute reply means nobody re-opened the question internally. It was
not considered and declined — it was closed.

## The three things this skill would have caught

**1. The counter was a single figure with nothing beside it.** The media-kit-only reply at stage
3 was right, and is not the mistake. The mistake is stage 5: they had $1,000 in writing and
answered with one number 3.4x higher and nothing to say yes to. **A lone counter reads as a
decline.** The buyer closes the thread rather than taking it back to their team, because you have
given them nothing to take.

**2. They had a $1,000 product and did not offer it.** A smaller package on their own rate card
was priced at exactly the number the brand had named. Days earlier, in a different thread, the
same creator made precisely the right move:

> "My rate for a dedicated video is $2,500, and I can't bring that down for this one. If $1,000
> is the ceiling for now, a Story Set of 3 would fit that."

Same week, same $1,000 ceiling, and the trade-down was offered to one and not the other. The
instinct was already there. It just did not fire under pressure.

**3. "Ads rights" is not "usage rights", and it was priced as if it were.** The brand asked for
30 days of *ads* rights — paid amplification, which is whitelisting territory, priced far higher
than ordinary usage. So the same message **overshot their budget and undercharged the rights at
once.** The fix is a question, not a number: what exactly do you intend to run, and where?

## What the skill would have handed them

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for coming back with a number, that helps.
>
> $1,000 doesn't reach a dedicated video. That's $2,500, and with 30 days of paid amplification
> on top it's $4,375.
>
> Two things that do work at $1,000:
>
> A Story Set of three, cross-posted, link in bio for seven days. Flat $1,000, no ads rights.
>
> Or hold the $1,000 against a video later in the year and I'll ringfence a slot for the launch.
>
> Which is more useful for you?
>
> Best,
> [name]

Headline rate untouched. A real thing they can buy today. Ends on a question rather than a number
they have to reject.

## The move to avoid, which is what happened

**Countering at 3.4x a stated budget with a single figure and no alternative.** It does not read
as firm, it reads as a decline. Firmness lives in holding your headline rate. Flexibility lives in
what else is on the menu.

## The wider pattern worth watching

Two brands the same week both landed on a **$1,000 ceiling**. Both died. That is a market signal,
not two coincidences: there was real demand at $1,000, and the only thing on the menu at that
price read as a consolation prize because it arrived second.

If two counterparties independently name the same number, that number is your market telling you
something. Build a deliberate product at it and offer it first, rather than climbing down to it.
